summary: Teaches the shared language of fractions, decimals and percentages: that 1/2, 0.5 and 50% are three notations for ONE value, and that the words (tenths/hundredths/thousandths, per cent, % symbol, convert, terminating decimal) must be USED correctly in context, not just recited. The load-bearing habits are place-value reading of decimals (0.09 can be read 'nine hundredths'; the digit reading 'zero point zero nine' is also conventional, but the place-value name shows what it means) and the 'out of 100' meaning of per cent (writing '9% of £420 = £37.80', never '9% = £37.80', while equivalences such as '9% = 0.09' remain correct). The flagship activity ties one shaded quantity to its fraction, decimal, percentage and number-line position so all forms move together; alternatives (matching/diagnostic practice, explaining to a younger child, a labelled reference display) exercise and check the same vocabulary with different affordances.
misconceptions: Reading decimals as digit strings ('point oh nine', 'point seven') instead of place-value names ('nine hundredths', 'seven tenths').
Treating fraction, decimal and percentage as different, unrelated things rather than three names for one value.
Misusing percentage notation — writing '10% = 42' instead of '10% of 420 = 42'.
Reading the percentage number as the whole ('50% means 50') rather than as parts per hundred.
Confusing per cent (out of 100) with a plain count.

activities.title: One quantity, three names — fill and watch them move together
steps: Fill a hundred square (or slide a bar) to show a chosen amount, e.g. drag to fill fifty squares.
Read the linked panel as it updates in lockstep: 50/100, 0.5, 50%, with a marker halfway along a 0%–100% number line.
Say the decimal aloud in place-value language ('five tenths, one half, fifty per cent'); use a 'read it' option to hear the correct reading.
Fill nine squares and confirm the panel reads 9/100, 0.09, 9% and voices the place-value name 'nine hundredths' alongside the digit reading 'zero point zero nine'.
Switch to context skins (a '9% off' price tag, a jug 0.5 full) and state the same fact as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
When finding part of an amount, practise saying and writing 'X% of N' (e.g. '9% of £420 = £37.80') rather than '9% = £37.80'; equivalences such as '9% = 0.09 = 9/100' are still correct.
activities.insight: A fraction, a decimal and a percentage are not three separate topics but one quantity wearing three names; the correct place-value reading and the 'per cent = out of 100' meaning are visible in the same moment the learner acts.

activities.title: Match, read and complete — diagnostic usage practice
steps: Match cards so that each value's three forms are grouped, e.g. 1/2 ↔ 0.5 ↔ 50%.
Choose the correct place-value reading of a decimal, e.g. 'What is the place-value name for 0.09?' with 'nine tenths' or 'nine' offered as tempting wrong answers.
Complete 'X% of N' statements, e.g. fill the blank in '__% of 420 = 42'.
Sort a mixed set of cards by the single value each one names.
activities.insight: Correct use of the vocabulary is checkable: the right place-value reading, the right grouping of equivalent forms, and the correct 'X% of N' phrasing distinguish understanding from digit-string reading and base-neglect.

activities.title: Explain it to a younger child
steps: Explain a shop's '9% off' sign or a half-full jug to a younger character who asks 'what does per cent mean?' and 'is that the same as a half?'
Say a single quantity three ways (fraction, decimal, percentage) and read each aloud correctly.
Answer whether '9% off' could ever take off more money than '50% off', and say what it depends on (the base amount).
activities.insight: Being pressed to explain forces the learner to produce and justify the three forms and the 'parts per hundred of a base' meaning in their own words.

activities.title: Four-way reference display
steps: Study one value shown four ways at once: shaded hundred square, fraction with denominator 100, decimal, and a point on a 0%–100% number line.
Tap each form to hear its correct reading (e.g. 'nine hundredths').
Open the flap on 'per cent = out of 100' to check the meaning.
activities.insight: Having the four parallel representations of one value side by side, each with its correct reading, gives a stable reference for the shared-value idea and place-value language.

checkQuestion: A jug is half full. Give me three different ways to say how full it is — as a fraction, as a decimal, and as a percentage — and read each one aloud the proper way. Then: a shop sign says '9% off a £420 coat'. Say what 9% means here, write it as a decimal, and tell me how much money comes off.
checkAnswer: Half full = 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, read as 'one half', 'five tenths / nought point five', 'fifty per cent'. 9% means nine out of every hundred (of the price); as a decimal 0.09; the money off is 9% OF £420, i.e. £37.80 (children may reason 1% of 420 = 4.20, so 9% = 37.80). The key usage: '9% of £420', never '9% = £37.80'.
